name: Raised fields, Lake Titicaca basin
summary: Platforms between water-filled canals on the high plain beside Lake Titicaca, farmed from about 1000 BCE, improved water control and gave some protection from frost at 3,800 metres.
description: Farmers on the seasonally flooded pampa beside Lake Titicaca, above 3,800 metres, built raised planting platforms separated by canals from about 1000 BCE, and the fields became part of the economic base of the Pukara culture. The canals conserved water and stored heat against frost. In the northern basin the fields fell out of use after about 300 CE, were rebuilt from about 1000 CE, and were probably in disuse by the time the Spanish arrived.

impact.note: The fields fed the societies of one high-altitude basin, where they made some 82,000 hectares of poor, flood-prone pampa farmable, a new capability there; nothing outside the basin is shown to descend from them.

date.label: c. 1000 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Raised-field agriculture around Lake Titicaca probably began around 1000 BCE, and was well established by 500 BCE.

evidence.supports: raised-field agriculture probably began around 1000 B.C., and was well established by 500 B.C.

date.label: c. 1000 CE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: After abandonment sometime after 300 CE, the raised fields of the Huatta pampa were rebuilt and reused from about 1000 CE until the Inca conquest of the lake zone sometime after 1450 CE.

evidence.supports: their abandonment occurred sometime after A.D. 300. The reconstruction and reutilization of these raised fields in Phase II probably began about A.D. 1000 and lasted until the Inca conquest of the lake zone sometime after A.D. 1450.
evidence.locator: End of the section before 'Discussion', p. 379

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Erickson's 2013 chapter is said to date the earliest fields to 1000-800 BCE and to associate them with the Chiripa and Qaluyu cultures; it was not read.
The extent and dating of Tiwanaku-period raised fields in the southern basin (Koani Pampa, Bolivia), and the lead's greatest extent of c. 500-1100 CE, were not checked.
Whether the fields arose independently of Maya and Amazonian wetland fields is not addressed by the source read.

research.note: Erickson's account covers the chronology and function of the fields but does not say whether they arose independently of other wetland fields, so independence is not established.
